findings.source_passage: Aloft, like a royal czar and king, the sun seemed giving this gentle air to this bold and rolling sea; even as bride to groom.
findings.why_it_matters: This sustained cosmological simile—sun as czar giving the feminine air to the masculine sea as bride to groom—is the rhetorical and interpretive keystone of the air/sea gender allegory that opens the chapter; its absence collapses the theological framing before Ahab even appears.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the sun-as-czar / bride-to-groom paragraph in full between the air/sea gender passage and Ahab's appearance.

findings.source_passage: Oh, immortal infancy, and innocency of the azure! Invisible winged creatures that frolic all round us! Sweet childhood of air and sky! how oblivious were ye of old Ahab's close-coiled woe!
findings.why_it_matters: This apostrophe is one of the chapter's most distinctively Melvillean rhetorical set-pieces and the interpretive counterpoint that frames Ahab's tragedy against cosmic innocence; its omission removes a critical ironic layer.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert the 'Oh, immortal infancy' apostrophe—at minimum the opening exclamations and the Miriam-and-Martha simile—between Ahab's appearance and his watching his shadow.

findings.source_passage: Slowly crossing the deck from the scuttle, Ahab leaned over the side and watched how his shadow in the water sank and sank to his gaze, the more and the more that he strove to pierce the profundity.
findings.why_it_matters: Ahab's shadow sinking as he tries to pierce the depths is one of the chapter's key symbolic images, read by critics as the projection of self into the abyss; its loss removes significant interpretive material.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the shadow-sinking sentence before the passage about aromas dispelling the cankerous thing in his soul.

findings.source_passage: the madness, the frenzy, the boiling blood and the smoking brow, with which, for a thousand lowerings old Ahab has furiously, foamingly chased his prey—more a demon than a man!—aye, aye!
findings.source_locator: Ahab's speech, mid-paragraph, after 'I widowed that poor girl'
findings.why_it_matters: This self-condemnatory climax—'more a demon than a man'—is the rhetorical peak of Ahab's self-awareness in the entire novel and a passage the critical tradition treats as central; its omission deflates the confessional arc of his speech.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the 'madness, the frenzy' sentence and 'more a demon than a man' within Ahab's monologue.

findings.source_passage: Starbuck saw the old man; saw him, how he heavily leaned over the side; and he seemed to hear in his own true heart the measureless sobbing that stole out of the centre of the serenity around.
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence—'measureless sobbing that stole out of the centre of the serenity around'—is one of the most celebrated prose passages in the chapter for its paradoxical beauty and is critical to establishing Starbuck's empathetic role; it is entirely replaced by a bare narrative tag.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Starbuck's approach paragraph verbatim, particularly 'the measureless sobbing that stole out of the centre of the serenity around.'

findings.source_passage: Look! see yon Albicore! who put it into him to chase and fang that flying-fish? Where do murderers go, man! Who's to doom, when the judge himself is dragged to the bar?
findings.source_locator: Ahab's final monologue, after the windlass sentence
findings.why_it_matters: These compressed rhetorical questions are distinctive voice markers that extend the fate/free-will meditation; their loss mildly thins the speech's philosophical texture.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the Albicore and 'Who's to doom' questions in Ahab's closing speech.

findings.source_passage: By the green land; by the bright hearth-stone! this is the magic glass, man; I see my wife and my child in thine eye.
findings.source_locator: Ahab's speech, near end, the 'magic glass' sentence
findings.why_it_matters: The 'magic glass' phrase and the hearth-stone oath are signature Melville diction; the draft omits them and jumps directly to 'I see my wife and my child,' losing the rhetorical build.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'By the green land; by the bright hearth-stone! this is the magic glass, man;' before 'I see my wife and my child in thine eye.'

summary: The draft preserves the chapter's frame and major speeches adequately but drops five medium-severity passages—the sun-as-czar allegory, the 'Oh, immortal infancy' apostrophe, Ahab's shadow sinking, 'measureless sobbing out of the centre of serenity,' and 'more a demon than a man'—each of which is critically engaged or voice-defining, triggering regeneration.
